title: CLO Tips — How to Create a Simple OBJ File in CLO, Using a Belt Buckle as an Example
description: CLO Tips — How to Create a Simple OBJ File in CLO, Using a Belt Buckle as an Example
transcript:
So I'm going to demonstrate how you can create an OBJ in Clo from scratch. You can make very simple OBJs or simple shapes. For anything very complicated, we recommend using an external 3D modeling software, but simple things like buttons or buckle shapes, D-rings, you can easily make in Clo.

I'm going to show you this process from beginning to end, starting by actually making the pattern piece or the shapes that I'm going to turn into an OBJ.

First, I'm going to make a small ring shape. I'll start by working in half increments. I'm going to make this 0.75 wide by... Actually, 0.75 is what I'll go with. This will be a very small piece, acting as a buckle. I'll zoom in so you can see what's happening as I work.

First, I'll round off my corners. I can type in the amount I want to round each corner. Great. Another thing with these very small pieces is that since we're not working with many elements in our workspace, you can work with a low particle distance. I'm going to change this to 5. A couple of pointers while doing this: when you export your pieces, you don’t want anything else in your workspace. In my case, I don’t have an avatar or a garment; I’m just creating the piece, and you’ll see why shortly.

I actually lowered my particle distance down to 2 to get better definition. I made half my shape, then I’m going to unfold it. I can delete some unnecessary points. I’m going to offset this outer edge as an internal line because I’m going to convert this to a hole. I could go with 1/8 inch, but maybe let’s make it a little thicker.

Okay, that looks good. I’ll hit OK. First, I want to check the measurement of the inner hole. Looks like I’m clearing just over an inch, which I’m happy with, so I’ll keep that.

Now I’ll convert this to a hole. From here, I want to kind of open up this shape more, so I can unfold this edge. This looks like one of those bra strap rings or a ring that might hold a belt closed.

So, to see what’s happening as I make changes, you should change your fabric view to Thick Textured Surface. I’m going to select the entire piece; with the whole piece selected, under Simulation Properties you’ll see something called Additional Thickness - Render. By default, it’s zero. This controls how thick the piece is. I can make it 4 millimeters thick, or 5, although that might be too thick. I want to see what 3.5 looks like, so I’ll keep it at 3.5.

The other thing we need to do is make the edges of this shape smoother, more rounded. Using either the Edit Pattern tool or the Transform Pattern tool, select the entire piece. In the Property Editor, under Selected Line, at the bottom you’ll see an option called Curved Side Geometry. I’ll open that so you can see.

Here it says Curved Side Geometry. You want to check this on. Once activated, all the hardware angles of the piece now turn into smooth curves. You can control the curvature percentage: if you decrease it, the edges become much flatter but still transition nicely from one edge to another. At zero, it looks like before turning it on; at 100, it’s very rounded. I’ll go somewhere a little below 100.

That looks good to me. Great. Now we have our piece. If I turned simulation on or tried to use this with a garment, it would still behave like fabric, not a hard object—it would crumple and drape like fabric. We need to export this as an OBJ and then bring it back in as the OBJ we exported.

To create and export: once your piece is ready, it’s very important not to have anything else in your workspace. I don’t have an avatar or garments. When everything is set, go to File > Export > choose OBJ. I’ll save this as “new OBJ buckle.” For this purpose, make sure Single Object is checked, and Thick is checked. Also, keep in mind the scale you’re exporting in. I’m exporting in centimeters, so when importing back, I’ll import in centimeters as well. Then click OK.

Once exported, you’ll get a zip file. You need to extract your OBJs from this zip file. I’m going to extract all and replace my file. Great.

Now that you have the OBJ file, I’ll show you how to add it to a garment. I have my garment here, and I’m going to put that buckle into this belt, at the front of the belt.

First, go to File > Import > Add. Make sure you choose Import Add, because it adds the object to your workspace. Locate the file and click Open. When you see this dialog box, you want to load this as an Avatar. There are two ways to load an OBJ: as an Avatar or as a Trim. For this case, load it as an Avatar for better properties to work with. Also, ensure the unit of measurement you import in matches what you exported. Click OK.

You’ll see it pop into your workspace. Using the Gizmo tool, move it to where you want it. This might take some maneuvering; it will just float or hover in space where you position it.

Once positioned where it looks good, start pulling your fabric through the opening. For this belt, which is small, again you can work on a lower particle distance. A couple of things to make this look more like a belt:

One, make your belt look thicker by adding additional thickness—I’ll type 1.5 millimeters. I’ve also applied curved side geometry to the edges. Then I’ll set this fabric to leather. That looks better now.

What we want to do next is pull this center area over the middle of our buckle. Using the Select Mesh tool, first, to get a reference of where the mesh part is, you can marquee over it in your 3D window; you’ll see that area turn green. Then go to your 2D window and grab the entirety of that area.

Once the appropriate area is selected, go to the 3D window, click on it. The Gizmo will pop up, and using the handles, you can pull that through. Once it’s through, turn simulation on, and you’ll see it start to settle.

A couple of things to improve the look: click on the OBJ, which has a property called Skin Offset. This acts as an invisible buffer to help keep pieces from melting into the avatar or the OBJ. Slowly reduce this value—about 0.5 at a time. I’ll type 2.5, simulate, then 2, then 1.5. You don’t want to go any lower than 0.5; try to keep it between 0.5 and 1. If you bring it to zero, the pattern pieces may start melting into the avatar. I’ll go down to 1. That looks good enough.

Great, now this looks nice. You can also add color to your OBJ—just click on it or use the color button and color picker if you prefer.

That’s it. If your pattern pieces are poking into your OBJ, try lowering the particle distance of those pieces in general.

And that’s it. You’re good to go.

chunks.title: CLO Tips — How to Create a Simple OBJ File in CLO, Using a Belt Buckle as an Example
chunks.content: ## Creating Simple OBJ Files in CLO Using a Belt Buckle Example This section explains how to create simple OBJ files directly within CLO, focusing on small hardware pieces like buckles, buttons, and D-rings. It covers pattern creation, shape editing, and exporting techniques optimized for 3D garment integration. ### Designing the Base Shape in CLO You can create simple OBJ shapes such as buckles and rings in CLO without external 3D software. For complex objects, external modeling tools are recommended, but small hardware components are manageable natively. - Start by designing half of the shape as a pattern piece. For example, create a ring by drafting half the shape with dimensions like 0.75 inches wide. - Round off corners by entering specific rounding values to smooth edges. - Use low particle distance values (e.g., 2 to 5) to increase mesh resolution for small pieces, improving definition. - Avoid having other elements like avatars or garments in your workspace during creation and export to prevent conflicts. ### Editing Pattern Details and Hole Creation - Unfold the half shape to full and delete unnecessary points. - Offset an outer edge inward to create an internal line that will become a hole. For instance, set the offset thickness to slightly more than 1/8 inch to achieve a hole diameter just over one inch. - Convert the offset internal line into a hole feature in CLO, essential for buckle ring openings. ### Adjusting Thickness and Edge Geometry - Switch Fabric View to "Thick Textured Surface" to preview thickness effects. - Under Simulation Properties, adjust "Additional Thickness - Render" to set the piece’s thickness (e.g., 3.5 mm for a buckle). - Smooth edges by enabling "Curved Side Geometry" in the Property Editor under Selected Line options. - Control curvature percentage to balance between flat edges and fully rounded corners (values close to 100% create smooth, rounded hardware edges). ### Exporting the OBJ File from CLO - Ensure the workspace contains only the OBJ piece, with no avatar or garments. - Export via File > Export > OBJ. - Set export options to: - Single Object: checked - Thick: checked (to preserve thickness in the export) - Confirm the export scale unit matches your working units (e.g., centimeters). - Exporting creates a ZIP file containing the OBJ, which must be extracted before import. --- ## Importing and Using the OBJ in CLO Garments This section covers importing the created OBJ back into CLO, positioning it within a garment, and integrating fabric simulation around the hardware piece. ### Importing the OBJ as an Avatar - Use File > Import > Add to bring the OBJ into the workspace. - Select "Import Add" to add the OBJ without replacing existing items. - When prompted, load the OBJ as an Avatar (not as a Trim) for better interaction and simulation properties. - Ensure unit settings on import match the export scale.

chunks.title: CLO Tips — How to Create a Simple OBJ File in CLO, Using a Belt Buckle as an Example
chunks.content: --- ## Importing and Using the OBJ in CLO Garments This section covers importing the created OBJ back into CLO, positioning it within a garment, and integrating fabric simulation around the hardware piece. ### Importing the OBJ as an Avatar - Use File > Import > Add to bring the OBJ into the workspace. - Select "Import Add" to add the OBJ without replacing existing items. - When prompted, load the OBJ as an Avatar (not as a Trim) for better interaction and simulation properties. - Ensure unit settings on import match the export scale. ### Positioning and Adjusting the OBJ - Use the Gizmo tool to move the OBJ into the desired location (e.g., front of a belt). - The OBJ will float in space; position it carefully for the best fit. ### Integrating Fabric with the OBJ - Set fabric properties of the garment piece around the OBJ: - Lower particle distance (e.g., 2-5) for better mesh detail near hardware. - Increase fabric thickness (e.g., 1.5 mm) for a bulky belt appearance. - Apply curved side geometry to fabric edges for smoothness. - Assign appropriate fabric type (e.g., leather) to enhance realism. - Pull fabric through the OBJ opening: - Select the mesh area in 3D view using the Select Mesh tool (marquee selection highlights the area). - In 2D view, select the corresponding pattern pieces. - Use Gizmo handles in 3D to move and pull the fabric through the buckle hole. - Turn on simulation to let the fabric settle naturally around the OBJ. ### Adjusting Skin Offset to Prevent Mesh Clipping - Select the OBJ and modify the "Skin Offset" property. - Skin Offset is an invisible buffer that prevents fabric or avatar mesh from intersecting the OBJ. - Reduce Skin Offset gradually in increments (e.g., 2.5 mm, 2 mm, 1.5 mm, down to no less than 0.5 mm). - Values below 0.5 mm risk mesh penetration and simulation artifacts. - Optimal Skin Offset is between 0.5 mm and 1 mm for realistic collision. ### Final Touches - Add color to the OBJ by selecting it and using the color picker or material properties. - If fabric pieces poke into the OBJ, lower their particle distance for higher mesh fidelity and better simulation detail. --- ## Summary Creating simple OBJ hardware components like buckles in CLO involves drafting precise pattern shapes, applying hole features, adjusting thickness and edge curvature, and exporting with correct settings. Importing as an Avatar allows proper positioning and interaction with garment fabrics. Adjusting simulation properties such as Skin Offset and particle distance ensures realistic integration without mesh clipping. This workflow enables the creation of custom hardware without external 3D modeling software for simple designs.
